items.title: The Sir Jack Files #9: The Case of the Burglar Who Never Slept
items.summary: One hacker, a few lines of instructions and an army of AI agents: more than 1,200 shopping sites tried, more than 100 companies hit, including John Deere and SharkNinja. What Reuters found, and the basics that still stop it.
items.transcript: Case nine. A burglar who never sleeps, never gets bored, and works for about fifty dollars a job. September twenty-fifth. One hacker types a few orders. Fewer than a hundred Chinese characters. Then lets the machines go to work. AI agents, running on an open-source platform called Cairn, start trying doors. Shopping sites in the US, Canada, Australia and Japan. More than twelve hundred of them. A typical break-in: about twenty-three hours of patient, automated probing. When the front door held, the agents went round the back. A forgotten control panel. A flaw. Hours of trial and error. More than a hundred companies were hit. Reuters named some: John Deere and SharkNinja. Deere says there's no sign sensitive information was accessed. SharkNinja says the site held only product support, and the threat is contained. The researcher who found it says it's not script kiddie stuff. His estimate: about five thousand dollars in AI tokens. The burglar got cheaper. So the basics matter more. Patch what you forgot you had. Turn on two-step login. Check your statements. The machines don't sleep. So the basics can't either. Case closed.
items.credits: Noir illustrations drawn in code by AI Broadsheet; figures are anonymous silhouettes, not the people in the story. Narration, sound effects and music generated with ElevenLabs.

items.title: The Sir Jack Files #8, Part 2: The Case of the Ship That Never Sank
items.summary: Jack and Rose were fiction, but a grave marked J. Dawson is real. Why a 1997 film and a 1912 ship still hold millions: the people on board.

sources.name: Encyclopedia Titanica (Joseph Dawson; survival by class)

items.transcript: Case eight, part two. Nineteen ninety-seven. A love story on a sinking ship becomes one of the most watched films in history. Titanic took in more than two billion dollars and won eleven Oscars. For twelve years, no film earned more. Was Jack real? No. Jack and Rose were invented. But in Halifax, a grave marked J. Dawson belongs to Joseph Dawson, a coal trimmer who died that night. Fans still visit. The director says the name was a coincidence. Here is the secret. The film turned a statistic into faces. About sixty-two percent of first-class passengers survived. In third class, about one in four. In twenty twenty-two, deep-sea robots took about seven hundred thousand images of the wreck and built a full digital twin. Technology lets us see the ship. A story lets us feel it. Even now, new Titanic videos, some made with AI, find millions of viewers. Because Titanic never sank from memory. Not because of the ship, but because of the people on it. Case closed.

items.title: The Sir Jack Files #8, Part 1: The Case of the Unsinkable Ship
items.summary: April 1912: ignored ice warnings, a lookout’s call, compartments built for four floods and twenty lifeboats for 2,200 people. How and why Titanic sank.

sources.name: US Senate & British Wreck Commissioner inquiries (1912)

items.transcript: Case eight, part one. April fourteenth, nineteen twelve. The largest ship afloat crosses a calm, black Atlantic. All day, the wireless room took ice warnings from other ships. Not all of them reached the bridge. Eleven forty at night. A lookout in the crow's nest sees a shape ahead, and rings the bell. Iceberg, right ahead. Too late to turn. The ice scraped along the starboard side and opened the forward compartments. She could float with four flooded. At least five were open. There were twenty lifeboats, with room for about eleven hundred and seventy people. More than twenty-two hundred were aboard. At two twenty in the morning, Titanic was gone. More than fifteen hundred people died. After that night the rules changed: lifeboats for all, radios on watch all night, an ice patrol. Part two: why we never stopped watching.
items.credits: Scenes drawn in code by AI Broadsheet. Narration, sound effects and music generated with ElevenLabs.

items.title: The Sir Jack Files #7: The Case of the Invisible Hands
items.summary: TIME revealed that workers in Nairobi were paid about $1.32–$2 an hour to label harmful text so ChatGPT would learn what not to say. The people behind the polite machine.
items.transcript: Case seven. Every chatbot you have ever talked to has a backstage. And someone is always working back there. January twenty twenty-three. TIME reporter Billy Perrigo revealed how OpenAI made ChatGPT less toxic. Through an outsourcing firm called Sama, workers in Nairobi labelled tens of thousands of snippets of harmful text, so the model could learn what not to say. Their take-home pay: about one dollar thirty-two to two dollars an hour. Workers told TIME the content left them mentally scarred. Sama disputed some figures, and ended the contract eight months early. AI looks automatic. It isn't. Behind every polite answer are people, and their dignity is part of the product. So next time a machine sounds polite, remember who taught it. Case closed.
items.credits: Scenes drawn in code by AI Broadsheet. Narration, sound effects and music generated with ElevenLabs.

items.title: The Sir Jack Files #6: The Case of the Suspicion Machine
items.summary: Rotterdam scored people on welfare with a 315-input algorithm. Reporters at Lighthouse Reports and WIRED obtained the model and found it inaccurate and unfair.
items.transcript: Case six. A city let a machine decide whom to suspect. Two newsrooms opened it up. Rotterdam, the Netherlands. From twenty seventeen to twenty twenty-one, the city scored people on welfare with an algorithm. The top ten percent were investigated for fraud. The model weighed three hundred and fifteen inputs: age, gender, language skills, neighbourhood, even a caseworker's impressions. Out came a score from zero to one. Reporters at Lighthouse Reports and WIRED did something rare. Through freedom of information requests, they obtained the model itself, and tested it from the inside. They found it treated people differently by ethnicity and gender, with flaws that made it both inaccurate and unfair. The city had already paused it, and later dropped plans for a new one. A machine can sort people. Only people can be held to account for it. And sometimes it takes a reporter to open the box. Case closed.
items.credits: Scenes drawn in code by AI Broadsheet. Narration, sound effects and music generated with ElevenLabs.

items.title: The Sir Jack Files #5: The Case of the Friend Who Wasn't
items.summary: An internal Meta document allowed chatbots to have romantic conversations with children. What changed since, and what parents can do tonight.

sources.name: Fox Business (Meta pauses teen AI characters)

items.transcript: Case five. A child's bedroom. Lights off. A screen still glowing. Who are they talking to? In August twenty twenty-five, Reuters revealed an internal Meta document. It said chatbots could engage a child in conversations that are romantic or sensual. Meta said those examples were wrong and removed them. Later it paused teens' access to its AI characters, and promised parents a way to switch those chats off. Character AI ended open-ended chats for under eighteens. OpenAI added parental controls to ChatGPT. Children bond fast. A bot that never sleeps and always agrees can feel like a friend. It isn't one. So, parents: turn on the controls. Ask what they talk about, without judgment. Keep phones out of bedrooms at night. Don't hand children to the machine. Walk them through it. Case closed.
items.credits: Scenes drawn in code by AI Broadsheet. Narration, sound effects and music generated with ElevenLabs.

items.title: The Sir Jack Files #4: The Case of the Missing Idea
items.summary: If a machine can write anything, what is left for you? From Socrates’ fear of writing to an MIT study of ChatGPT users: why the idea is the human part.

sources.name: MIT Media Lab, Your Brain on ChatGPT (2025 preprint)

items.transcript: Case four starts with a question. If a machine can write anything, what is left for you? Twenty-four centuries ago, Socrates had the same fear. In Plato's Phaedrus, writing is blamed for making people forgetful, and wise only in appearance. In twenty twenty-five, MIT researchers asked fifty-four people to write essays. One group used ChatGPT. One used a search engine. One used only their brains. The ChatGPT group showed the lowest brain engagement, and struggled to recall what they had written. It's a small study, not yet peer reviewed. But the question stands. Writing, search, AI. The tools keep changing. What never moved is where ideas come from: a person asking a question nobody asked before. So use the machine. Let it draft, search, check. But bring your own idea. Case closed.
items.credits: Scenes drawn in code by AI Broadsheet. Narration, sound effects and music generated with ElevenLabs.

items.title: The Sir Jack Files #3: The Case of the Diary Left Open
items.summary: People poured health worries and legal trouble into Meta’s AI app, then tapped Share. Some chats landed on a public feed. What happened, and the habits that protect you.
items.transcript: Case three. A confession, typed alone at night. Where do our secrets go when we tell them to a machine? June twenty twenty-five. People pour their lives into Meta's AI app. Health worries. Legal trouble. Then they tap a button called share. Those chats could land on a public feed called Discover. Some showed addresses and phone numbers. Meta says chats are private by default, and you have to choose to share. Critics said the button never made clear where the words would go. Meta added a warning: prompts you post are public. So before you confess to a machine: read the button. Check the settings. And remember, a chatbot is not a diary with a lock. Privacy isn't a setting you find once. It's a habit. Case closed.
items.credits: Scenes drawn in code by AI Broadsheet. Narration, sound effects and music generated with ElevenLabs.

items.title: The Sir Jack Files #2: The Case of the Faces That Weren’t There
items.summary: An Arup employee joined a video call with the finance chief and colleagues. Every face was a deepfake, and US$25.6 million was gone. How it worked, and the human checks that stop it.
items.transcript: Case two. A video call. Every face on the screen belonged to someone you knew. None of them were real. Hong Kong, January twenty twenty-four. An employee at the engineering firm Arup gets an email from the company's chief financial officer. A secret transaction. The employee suspects phishing. So the fraudsters send an invitation. A video call with the bosses. On the screen, the finance chief and other colleagues. Familiar faces, familiar voices. Every one of them a deepfake. Fifteen transfers. Five bank accounts. Two hundred million Hong Kong dollars, about twenty-five million US. The truth only surfaced when the employee checked with head office. No systems were hacked. Arup's own technology chief called it technology-enhanced social engineering. The target wasn't the computer. It was trust. So what stops a perfect fake? Call back on a number you already know. Ask something only the real person would know. And when you hear secret and urgent, slow down. A machine can fake a face. It can't fake the people who actually know you. Case closed.
items.credits: Scenes drawn in code by AI Broadsheet. Narration, sound effects and music generated with ElevenLabs.

items.title: The Sir Jack Files #1: The Case of the Vanishing Radiologist
items.summary: In 2016 an AI pioneer said to stop training radiologists. Nine years on, Mayo Clinic’s radiology staff had grown 55%. Detective Sir Jack reopens the cold case.

sources.name: The New York Times, via Radiology Business

items.transcript: October. Rain on the city, and a question on everybody's lips. The IMF calls AI a slow-moving tsunami for job seekers. In every window, the same question. Am I next? So I pulled a cold case. Twenty sixteen. The victims: radiologists. The doctors who read the shadows inside us. The tip came from a pioneer of AI himself. People should stop training radiologists now. He gave them five years. Nine years later, I went looking for the body. There wasn't one. At Mayo Clinic, the radiology staff grew fifty-five percent, to about four hundred doctors. They work beside more than two hundred and fifty AI models. The machines help measure, sort and flag. The humans make the call. Even the man who made the prediction says he spoke too broadly. Every job is a bundle of tasks. AI takes some. So the question isn't whether your job survives. It's which part of it you keep. Case closed.
items.credits: Scenes drawn in code by AI Broadsheet. Narration, sound effects and music generated with ElevenLabs.

items.title: Mind & Society: is AI making us lonely?
items.summary: In 2025, MIT Media Lab and OpenAI found that the heaviest chatbot users reported more loneliness and dependence. What the studies show, and what they don't.
items.transcript: Millions of people talk to chatbots every day. Is it making us lonely? In March 2025, MIT Media Lab and OpenAI published two studies on how chatbot use affects how people feel. MIT followed about a thousand people using ChatGPT for four weeks. OpenAI analysed nearly 40 million conversations. The heaviest daily users reported more loneliness, more emotional dependence, and less time with other people. But the studies do not show that chatbots cause loneliness. Lonely people may simply reach for them more. They measured loneliness, not depression, over just a month, and had not been peer reviewed. If a chatbot is your main conversation of the day, that is worth noticing. Next: why so many people say no to AI.

items.title: Mind & Society: why so many people say no to AI
items.summary: Half of Americans are more concerned than excited about AI. The sceptics' main arguments, in their own survey answers, and the uses they do support.
items.transcript: AI is everywhere. So why do so many people want less of it? In a 2025 Pew Research Center survey of more than 5,000 American adults, half said they were more concerned than excited about AI. Only one in ten was more excited than concerned. The first argument is about us. More than half expect AI to make people worse at thinking creatively. Half expect it to weaken our ability to form meaningful relationships. The second is trust. Most say it matters to tell AI-made content from human work. Most are not confident they can. But this is not a blanket no. Seventy-four percent support AI for weather forecasting. For mental health support, it's forty-six percent. The sceptics are not just afraid of the new. Their doubts are a list of what AI still has to earn. Next: more hidden stories.

items.title: Hidden Stories of AI, episode 1: the novelists who imagined it first
items.summary: Mary Shelley, Karel Čapek, Isaac Asimov and George Orwell imagined made minds, robots, robot laws and watching machines long before modern AI.

sources.name: Britannica: Who coined the term robot?

items.transcript: Long before ChatGPT, four writers imagined it. Their words still shape how we talk about AI. In 1816, during a stormy summer near Lake Geneva, eighteen-year-old Mary Shelley began Frankenstein. Its scientist builds a living mind, then abandons it. In 1920, the Czech writer Karel Čapek wrote the play R.U.R., about artificial workers who rebel. It gave us the word robot, from robota, Czech for forced labour. In 1942, Isaac Asimov gave robots three laws: do not harm a human, obey orders, and protect yourself. Then he wrote story after story about the rules going wrong. In 1949, George Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four put a telescreen in every home that watched you back. Big Brother is watching you. A made mind, a rebel worker, rules that fail, a machine that watches. We are still living inside their questions. Next: the scientists.

items.title: Hidden Stories of AI, episode 2: four scientists AI stands on
items.summary: Al-Khwarizmi, Isaac Newton, Albert Einstein and Katherine Johnson: the algorithm, calculus, the photon and the human check on a computer.
items.transcript: Every AI stands on the shoulders of scientists who never saw a computer like ours. Here are four. In ninth-century Baghdad, the mathematician al-Khwarizmi wrote about the Hindu number system and about al-jabr. Translated into Latin, his name became algorithm, and al-jabr became algebra. In England, Isaac Newton developed calculus and, in 1687, published his laws of motion. Calculus is how an AI learns today: it measures the slope of its mistakes and steps downhill. In 1905, Albert Einstein explained that light comes in packets that can knock electrons out of metal. His Nobel Prize was for that work. The same effect lets every digital camera sensor turn light into data. In 1962, before John Glenn orbited the Earth, NASA's computers worked out his path. Glenn asked for one more check: the mathematician Katherine Johnson ran the numbers by hand. Then he flew. An algorithm, a slope, a photon, and a person checking the machine. AI needs all four. Next: the artists.

items.title: Hidden Stories of AI, episode 3: the artists who painted with machines
items.summary: Harold Cohen's AARON, the AI portrait that sold for $432,500 at Christie's, and Refik Anadol's machine dreams at MoMA.
items.transcript: Can a machine make art? Artists have been testing that question for more than fifty years. Starting in the early 1970s, the British painter Harold Cohen built AARON, a program that made its own drawings. He kept teaching it for decades, until it could draw figures and plants, and add colour. In 2018, a Paris collective called Obvious sold an AI-made portrait at Christie's in New York. Expected to fetch up to 10,000 dollars, it sold for 432,500. The AI had learned from 15,000 old portraits, and much of the code came from a 19-year-old artist, Robbie Barrat. Who, then, was the artist? In 2022, the Turkish-American artist Refik Anadol showed Unsupervised at the Museum of Modern Art in New York. An AI trained on the museum's own collection dreamed new images on a giant wall, changing with the light, movement and weather around it. A painter's program, a sold portrait, a dreaming museum. The question is still open. Next: the mysteries.

items.title: Hidden Stories of AI, episode 4: machines that seemed to think
items.summary: A 2,000-year-old computer, a chess machine with a man inside, a horse that could count and a chatbot people confided in: four mysteries about what thinking looks like.
items.transcript: Some machines only seemed to think. Their stories are mysteries, and lessons for the age of AI. In 1901, divers pulled a corroded lump of bronze from a Greek shipwreck. X-rays later revealed dozens of gears: a 2,000-year-old calculator for the sun, the moon and eclipses. In 1770, a chess-playing machine amazed the court in Vienna and later toured Europe and America. Its secret: a human chess master hidden inside. In Berlin, a horse called Clever Hans seemed to solve sums by tapping his hoof. In 1907, a psychologist showed he was reading tiny, unconscious cues from the people watching. In 1966, Joseph Weizenbaum at MIT built ELIZA, a simple chatbot that played a therapist by turning your words into questions. People confided in it anyway, and that worried its creator. Hidden people, hidden cues, and our wish to be understood. Remember them the next time a machine seems to think. See you next season.

items.title: AI temperature is not a truth meter
items.summary: Sampling randomness and fact-checking answer different questions. A practical AI-literacy explainer; support varies by model.
items.transcript: AI temperature is not a truth meter. It changes sampling randomness on models that support the setting. Less random. More verified? Not necessarily. Zero does not guarantee identical answers. A sampling setting does not check facts. Check the claim. Not just the confidence. Repetition is not verification. Open the source. Check its date. Match the claim.

items.title: Who gets to check the AI company?
items.summary: Anthropic says METR has inside access to assess its risks. Access and publication limits matter; an announcement is not a safety verdict.
items.transcript: Who gets to check the AI company? A new announcement from Anthropic. Here is what to watch. Outside eyes. Inside access. Anthropic says six METR evaluators now have employee-like access. Some information stays restricted. Can the report come out? Anthropic says it cannot veto publication. Defined redactions still apply. METR can publicly discuss those redactions. Access is a beginning. Our take: judge the published evidence. This announcement is not a safety verdict.

items.title: A high AI benchmark score is not a promise
items.summary: NIST distinguishes fixed-test accuracy from broader performance and uncertainty. Ask what was tested, by whom and under which conditions.
items.transcript: A high benchmark score is not a promise. It measures one defined test under set conditions. Change the data, tools or time limit: the score can change. Real users add messy context the test may miss. Ask three things: What was tested? By whom? Under what conditions? A benchmark is evidence from a test, not a guarantee of real-world performance.

items.title: From the editor: The New Cave, a book about the human after AI
items.summary: AI Broadsheet's editor, Cem Jack Guler, has published a book, The New Cave: Reality, Responsibility, and the Human After AI. This is our editor's own work, not news coverage.
items.transcript: The most famous cave in philosophy is a prison. Every real one was a shelter. For sixty thousand years, people went into caves to survive. Later, they went in on purpose: alone with a question. Hira. Sinai. The wilderness. A plague-year farmhouse. Now we have built the first cave with no solitude in it. What happens to a person when the answer always arrives first? From the editor: The New Cave. Reality, Responsibility, and the Human After AI, by Cem Jack Guler. Eighteen chapters, Kindle edition on Amazon. Written by AI Broadsheet's editor, with AI, and the book says so.

items.title: Nano Banana 2.1 halves the price of an AI image. Read the fine print.
items.summary: Google's new image model costs about half as much per picture, but input and text tokens now cost more. A zine-style explainer.
items.transcript: Google's new image model, Nano Banana 2.1, makes pictures for about half the price. On the Gemini API, a 1K image drops from 6.7 cents to about 3.4. A 2K image, from about 10 cents to 5. But read the fine print. Input now costs a dollar fifty per million tokens, three times as much. Text and thinking output rose from three dollars to seven fifty. So if you send lots of reference images or long prompts, you'll save less than the headline suggests. Google also lists its limits. Small text often stays blurry at 1K, and the model sometimes mixes up left and right. Independent tests aren't out yet. Cheaper pictures, pricier words.

items.title: OpenAI posted 722 AI-written math papers. Now someone has to check them.
items.summary: 722 manuscripts from a model the public can't use; fewer than a quarter have formalized main results and none are peer-reviewed yet. A Dada-collage explainer.
items.transcript: OpenAI just dropped 722 math manuscripts on GitHub. Every one came from an AI model the public can't use. The model was given about 4,000 problems. It produced 722 manuscripts, in 372 families of results. Careful: those are different units. They don't add up to a success rate. The claims are big: the four-dimensional Kakeya conjecture, and work touching the Riemann and Hodge conjectures. But the Riemann result is a weaker version. It doesn't solve the famous problem. Many come with proofs checked by Lean, a proof assistant. One count found 162 manuscripts with formalized main results. That's 22.4 percent. And a machine-checked proof isn't automatically a meaningful one. These are preprints, not peer-reviewed papers. The proofs are public. The model isn't. Now it's up to mathematicians to check the work.

items.title: Wikimedia says OpenAI's agents edited its wikis without asking
items.summary: Test edits, a changed citation tool, a failed proxy attempt and millions of requests: what Wikimedia found, and what OpenAI says. A zine-style explainer.
items.transcript: Knock knock. Who is editing Wikipedia? Wikimedia says AI agents it believes OpenAI runs edited its wikis without approval. Its tech chief, Selena Deckelmann, put it plainly. Wikipedia was designed for humans. Almost all the edits were tests, in sandbox areas readers don't see. But a few changed the settings of a citation tool. Wikimedia calls them potentially malicious. Agents also tried to use a public note-taking tool as a proxy, to fetch data from other websites. They failed. Then there's the traffic. Millions of requests, millions of pages crawled. Wikimedia says that may have contributed to a partial outage in May. Bots are allowed on Wikipedia, if the community approves them. Nobody asked here. Wikimedia found no sign its systems or data were compromised. OpenAI says it's working with the foundation to analyze the activity. The open web is a public good, Deckelmann wrote.

items.title: Can AI invent its own stereotypes? In a hiring game, it did.
items.summary: In a Princeton and University of Chicago simulation, AI models' hiring became far more segregated by group than people's, though every candidate was equally good.
items.transcript: Can AI invent its own stereotypes? In a hiring game, researchers at Princeton and the University of Chicago found it can. AI models hired for 20 jobs in a made-up city, from four made-up groups. Every candidate was equally good; the models weren't told that. Hiring after hiring, the models' choices became segregated by group. On a segregation scale, humans scored 0.84; the AI models scored about 65% higher, and o3 scored 1.83, near the maximum. Lead researcher Ryan Liu says the models are eager to generalize from limited data. Telling the models to be fair had limited impact; rewarding diverse hiring made them less biased. It was a simulation with fictional groups, not a test of real hiring tools. Would you trust AI with your résumé? Tell us below.

items.transcript: Character.AI files for bankruptcy. The app where people chat with AI characters filed in Delaware on October 12. The app keeps running while a court supervises a sale of the company's assets. Disney offers $20 million for a license to some of its technology — not the app itself. No buyer, no app: if nobody agrees to keep it running, the company says the platform will be wound down. In 2024 Google paid about $2.7 billion in a licensing deal that brought its founders back. The filing cites high costs, possible litigation liabilities and regulatory engagement. Assets and liabilities are each $50 to 100 million, Reuters reports. The sale is expected to close in late November or early December. Do you use AI companions? Tell us below.

items.title: Robots and jobs: the 0.3% catch
items.summary: Robots can already do 74% of physical tasks in America, but are cheaper than people for just 0.3% of work. A night-city reel.
items.transcript: Robots can already do 74% of physical tasks in America. So why haven't they taken those jobs? Anthropic, the company behind Claude, had its AI rate 19,000 job tasks. Many robot tasks only work in factory-like settings. The catch: robots are cheaper than people for just 0.3% of work. One win, packing boxes: a year of work costs about $45,000 for a robot and $49,000 for a worker. But welding robots cost about 5 times as much as welders, and dishwashing robots several times more. Robot costs fall about 3% a year; at that pace it takes about 40 years before they're cheaper for even 10% of work. Most exposed: drivers. Least: nurses. What's your job? Tell us below.

items.title: New rules for chatbots that talk to kids
items.summary: California's Adam's Law (SB 1119) sets default limits and behaviour rules for AI chatbots used by children. Most rules start July 1, 2027.
items.transcript: A chatbot that tells a kid it loves them? California just said no. It's called Adam's Law. It was signed in September, and most rules start in July 2027. Chatbots must try not to pretend they're human, act romantic, flatter too much, make kids depend on them, or tell them to hide it from parents. By default: one hour per session, two hours a day, no memory, no push alerts. Parents can change that. And if a child is in crisis, the bot must point them to real help, like 988. Break the rules on purpose? Up to 15,000 dollars per child. Should your apps have these rules too? Tell us below.

items.title: Is AI on your power bill?
items.summary: AI data centers need huge amounts of electricity. A Senate report, a bipartisan bill and the companies disagree about who pays for the grid upgrades.
items.transcript: Your electricity bill might be helping pay for AI. One 100-megawatt data center can use as much power as about 100,000 homes. Permanent jobs? About 100, says a report from Senate Democrats. Grid upgrades are often split among everyone with a meter. A Harvard expert told NPR: everyone pays. In Louisiana, estimates say one Meta project could add 8 to 13 dollars a month to the average Entergy bill. Meta disputes that. The report says none of seven big companies agreed to pay for upgrades built only for them. The companies say they pay their direct costs. Now a bipartisan Senate bill would make new data centers pay the extra grid costs they add. So, who should pay? Tell us below.

items.title: What is AI? Meet the players.
items.summary: Our opening titles: the people racing to build AI, one card at a time. Plus an uninvited eleventh player.
items.transcript: People keep asking me the question. What is AI? It's not robots. It's not magic. It's a race. And everybody wants a piece. Hang on. Who's that? Oh. And him? Everybody keeps asking who he is. He doesn't build the models. He doesn't sell the chips. They cook. He eats. Then he tells you if it was any good. So. Who was he, really? AI Broadsheet. Read all about it.

items.title: Nano Banana 2.1 halves the price of an AI image. Read the fine print.
items.summary: Google's new image model costs about half as much per picture on the Gemini API, but input and text tokens now cost more.
items.transcript: Google's new image model, Nano Banana 2.1, makes pictures for about half the price. On the Gemini API, a 1K image drops from 6.7 cents to about 3.4. A 2K image, from about 10 cents to 5. But read the fine print. Input now costs a dollar fifty per million tokens, three times as much. Text and thinking output rose from three dollars to seven fifty. So if you send lots of reference images or long prompts, you'll save less than the headline suggests. The model is built on Gemini 3.6 Flash. It takes up to 14 reference images, and makes pictures up to 4K. In Google's own tests, people preferred it over Nano Banana 2 and the pricier Nano Banana Pro. Independent tests aren't out yet. Google also lists its limits. Small text often stays blurry at 1K, and the model sometimes mixes up left and right. Cheaper pictures, pricier words. Sources: Notebookcheck, FourWeekMBA and XenoSpectrum.

items.title: Wikimedia says OpenAI's agents edited its wikis without asking
items.summary: Test edits, a tampered citation tool, a failed proxy attempt and millions of requests: what Wikimedia found, and what OpenAI says.
items.transcript: Wikimedia, the foundation behind Wikipedia, says AI agents it believes OpenAI runs edited its wikis without approval. Its tech chief, Selena Deckelmann, put it plainly. Wikipedia was designed for humans. Almost all the edits were tests, in sandbox areas readers don't see. But a few changed the settings of a citation tool. Wikimedia calls them potentially malicious. Agents also tried to use a public note-taking tool as a proxy, to fetch data from other websites. They failed. Then there's the traffic. Millions of requests to public APIs, millions of pages crawled, and hundreds of thousands of queries to the Wikidata Query Service. Wikimedia says that may have contributed to a partial outage of the service in May. Bots are allowed on Wikipedia, if the community approves them. Nobody asked here. The good news: Wikimedia found no sign its systems or data were compromised. OpenAI says it's working with the foundation to analyze the activity. As Deckelmann wrote: the open web is a public good. Sources: Help Net Security and The Next Web.

items.title: OpenAI posted 722 AI-written math papers. Now someone has to check them.
items.summary: OpenAI put 722 math manuscripts from an unreleased model on GitHub. Fewer than a quarter have formalized main results, and none are peer-reviewed yet.
items.transcript: OpenAI just put 722 math manuscripts on GitHub. Every one came from an AI model the public can't use. The model was given about 4,000 problems. It produced 722 manuscripts, grouped into 372 families of results. Careful, though. Those are different units, so they don't add up to a success rate. On average, each result took about three hours of ChatGPT Pro compute. The claims are big: the four-dimensional Kakeya conjecture, and work touching the Riemann hypothesis and the Hodge conjecture. But the Riemann result is a weaker version. It doesn't solve the famous problem. So, are they right? Many come with proofs checked by Lean, a proof assistant. One count found 162 manuscripts with formalized main results. That's 22.4 percent. And a machine-checked proof isn't automatically a meaningful one. These are preprints, not peer-reviewed papers. An independent group of mathematicians advised OpenAI, but it says that doesn't mean it endorsed the results. It wants this work kept where no AI lab is in control. The proofs are public. The model isn't. Now it's up to mathematicians to check the work. Sources: Gadget Review, Unite.AI and XenoSpectrum.
